newsitem.title: MEXICO: MEXICO DEBT OUTLOOK - Analysts say shun Cetes.
newsitem.headline: MEXICO DEBT OUTLOOK - Analysts say shun Cetes.

text.p: Recent declines in Cetes interest rates, coupled with the prospect of a sharp post-election peso depreciation, have diminished the appeal of the Mexican treasury bills, investment bank debt analysts said Thursday.

But the country's improving economic picture is providing a strong backdrop for its sovereign external debt, prompting debt analysts to recommend buying those instruments instead, the analysts said Thursday.
"Rates have been coming down pretty consistantly, and the peso has strengthened, so we don't find the Cetes that attractive," said Bear Stearns debt analyst Tulio Vera.
Analysts are also saying the currency could weaken after July mid-term elections, raising the risk of holding Cetes.

Salomon Brothers said the Mexican authorities may keep the currency stable in the run up to the July elections, but a sharp step-like adjustment in the exchange rate after a period of stability could come soon after.

"On that basis, a neutral to underweight allocation is recommended with respect to Mexican local currency instruments, especially since 28-day Cetes have reached recent historic lows," Salomon said in a report.
The bellwether 28-day Cetes rate fell 84 basis points at Banco de Mexico's auction on Tuesday to reach 18.07 percent.
Moreover, those rates could remain volatile.

Press reports this week said Mexico's central bank was running an inflationary monetary policy before the upcoming elections, although various economists and the central bank have vigorously disputed that theory.
Brokerage house Abaco said the central bank's actions pointed instead at an effort to keep rates from falling even further in secondary markets.
"Our feeling is that rates will remain somewhat volatile in the short-term, with the possibility of some upward spikes in the coming weeks," Abaco said.
Longer-term foreign denominated debt, however, is another story.
"Mexico certainly looks very good in comparison to the rest of Latin America," said Desmond Lachman, head of global emerging markets economic research for Salomon Brothers.
"The economic fundamentals are rather good," he said, pointing to a number of factors including an improving balance-of-payments, lower inflation, and good budget numbers.

Salomon Brothers said in a report that their overweight recommendation on Mexico's long-term sovereign bonds is based on a relatively benign economic environment that should outweigh political noise associated with upcoming elections.
Mexicans will vote for a new lower house in Congress on July 6, as well as part of the Senate, governors in six states and the mayor of Mexico City.
Another factor in the positive sentiments is a recent rally in Brady bonds on rumors of another buyback.
Since any such buyback remains speculative, another strategy would be to buy medium to long-term Mexican Eurobonds, said Bear Stearns' Vera.

"Accordingly, we recommend UMS '16, BNCE '06, and CFE '03," he said in a report. "One trade we like in Mexico is swapping out of UMS '07 and into BNCE '06, for a pick up of 55 basis points and reduction of effective duration."
((--Mexico City newsroom 525 728-9559))
